newsitem.title: ARMENIA: New Armenian PM denies harder line on Azerbaijan.
newsitem.headline: New Armenian PM denies harder line on Azerbaijan.

text.p: New Armenian Prime Minister Robert Kocharyan on Tuesday denied his recent shock appointment meant a harder stance by his country on its long-running territorial conflict with neighbour Azerbaijan.

Kocharyan, until recently president of the breakaway Azeri region of Nagorno-Karabakh, was named to the post last Thursday by President Levon Ter-Petrosyan in a move which came as a surprise in both Armenia and Azerbaijan.

Nagorno-Karabakh, entirely within Moslem Azerbaijan's borders but populated mostly by ethnic Armenians, broke away from Baku's rule in the late 1980s. Fighting killed thousands before a ceasefire was declared three years ago.

Diplomats and observers have interpreted Kocharyan's appointment as a hardening of the Armenian stance on the nine-year-old dispute, the oldest ethnic conflict in the former Soviet Union and one which helped hasten its demise.

"I don't think this (my appointment) will have any effect on the Karabakh question," he said in his first meeting with journalists since the appointment. "This is just what Azerbaijan says. Whatever happens in Armenia, Azerbaijan always sees as a problem."
Kocharyan conceded he had no new ideas on how to solve the intractable conflict, which some fear could erupt into new bloodshed.
"Our position is grounded in historical factors. I have no new suggestions. Our old ones have not been realised yet," said the slender, slightly low-key 43-year-old.

Azerbaijan says it will never recognise the region's declared independence or its right to join Armenia proper. But it has no control over Karabakh and analysts say it is not at present capable of carrying out a successful war to recapture it.

The Azeri military fared miserably during the conflict, losing all of the breakaway territory as well as a huge buffer zone carved out around it by Armenian fighters. Azerbaijan is now awash with hundreds of thousands of refugees.
Baku makes no secret of its plans to use revenues from huge, untapped offshore Caspian Sea oil reserves to build a military machine capable of retaking lost lands if peace talks fail to bear fruit.
The Azeri government has previously avoided direct talks with the Karabakh leadership, saying the matter should be resolved between it and Yerevan directly.
Kocharyan shed little light on why the aloof 51-year-old president Ter-Petrosyan had named him as his sixth prime minister in as many years in power.

Some observers have suggested Ter-Petrosyan sought to court favour with nationalist and opposition forces who see his rule as illegitimate. They allege he rigged last year's presidential election, in which he won a narrow first-round victory.

Ter-Petrosyan sent tanks into the streets of the capital for several days and rounded up dozens of political foes after demonstrations over the vote -- which foreign monitors said was marred by fraud and irregularities -- turned violent.

Kocharyan said the prospects for peace talks sponsored by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) were dim, but that his arrival on the scene, as someone directly involved in the conflict, might bring a new impetus.
"Let's put it this way. The talks have been in a dead end for a long time. We've been looking for a way out of it for a year and a half," he said.
"I want to assist this process. Perhaps we can move the talks from a standstill. I am hoping this can happen."

The group of foreign nations leading international attempts to reach a settlement on Karabakh urged both sides on Tuesday to "accelerate negotiations, avoid propagandistic statements and create a good atmosphere for the peace process".
The United States, Russia and France, which jointly chair the Minsk Group of mediators, issued the statement in Yerevan.
